title: On‑Prem TF Module Install & Runtime Troubleshooting Runbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This is a compact, action-oriented runbook for dealing with common install and runtime failures observed in private (VPC / on‑prem) deployments that use our Terraform modules. It is intentionally conversational and checklist-driven — copy sections into incident tickets or Slack threads while triaging. Draft: expect incomplete links and local notes.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: SREs, infra engineers, solutions eng doing customer installs, and engineers on private deployments on‑call.
- Scope: TF module install failures, TF plan/apply issues, runtime startup errors for the Redwood serving runtime (systemd/k8s), and quick smoke tests to validate a repaired install. Not a replacement for the full runbook in Confluence, but a practical troubleshooting cheat‑sheet.

Quick triage (0–10 minutes):
1) Confirm the symptom: failing terraform apply? runtime service crash? model load OOM? API 500s? capture the short summary.
2) Gather basics: customer, region, node types (GPU/CPU), TF workspace name, tfstate location (s3/gs/blob), last successful apply timestamp.
3) Check state lock: `terraform plan` fails with lock? run `terraform force-unlock` only after confirming no concurrent user.
4) If runtime is down: check node health (ping, SSH) and systemd or container runtime logs (commands below).

Essential commands (safe sequences):
- Terraform: `terraform init -upgrade` then `terraform validate` then `terraform plan -out=tfplan` (capture plan output).
- Remote state: `aws s3api get-object --bucket X --key path/to/state .` or use `terraform state pull` for manual inspection.
- Lock handling: `terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>` only if you are certain.
- System services: `sudo journalctl -u redwood-runtime -n 200 --no-pager` and `sudo systemctl status redwood-runtime`.
- Containers / k8s: `docker ps -a --filter name=redwood` or `kubectl -n redwood get pods` then `kubectl -n redwood logs <pod> --previous` for crash loops.
- GPU checks: `nvidia-smi` for visibility, `dmesg | grep -i nvidia` for drivers, and check driver/kernel mismatches in `/var/log/messages`.

Smoke test checklist (post‑repair): run these in order and mark PASS/FAIL quickly. Keep outputs in incident notes.
- Infra: `ssh` to each node that was part of the change.
- Services: `systemctl is-active redwood-runtime` (should be active).
- Health endpoints: curl `http://localhost:8080/healthz` and `http://localhost:8080/readyz` from node and from an app‑facing network hop.
- End‑to‑end inference: send a tiny sample payload to the model router with a short prompt and verify 200 + reasonable tokens returned.
- Latency sanity: single‑token genie: measure p50 < expected threshold (customer baseline).
- KV cache warmup: confirm KV cache hits rising after repeated requests (if enabled).
- Metrics: check Prometheus for exporter up=1, model-serving clients reporting active sessions.

Common failure patterns and quick root causes:
1) Terraform plan/apply errors after provider upgrades
   - Symptom: provider plugin mismatch, unknown resource type, or diffs that look like provider semantic changes.
   - Quick checks: `terraform providers` and pinned provider versions in `required_providers` in root module.
   - Workaround: pin provider to last known good version, re-run `terraform init -upgrade=false`, re-plan.

2) Remote state corruption / partial apply
   - Symptom: some resources created but tfstate shows drift or missing resources; subsequent applies error with existing resources.
   - Quick checks: inspect remote state (`terraform state pull`), list cloud resources, check backend storage object versioning.
   - Workaround: import conflicting resources into state (`terraform import`) or restore prior state snapshot from backend and reapply.

3) Lock stuck on CI or crash on apply
   - Symptom: `Error: Error locking state: NoSuchKey` or stale lock ID.
   - Quick checks: backend storage for lock file and check CI runners.
   - Workaround: coordinate with CI, use force-unlock if safe.

4) Kernel/NVIDIA driver mismatch causing GPU allocation failures
   - Symptom: runtime fails to create CUDA context, model-serving containers exit with driver error, `nvidia-smi` missing.
   - Quick checks: `nvidia-smi`, `modinfo nvidia`, driver package vs kernel version.
   - Workaround: roll driver back or upgrade kernel consistently, restart docker/kubelet.

5) File permission / SELinux denials preventing runtime from reading artifacts
   - Symptom: permission denied on model.tar or mounts failing, SELinux AVC denials in audit logs.
   - Quick checks: `ls -l` on mountpoints, `ausearch -m avc -ts recent`, `journalctl` for mounts.
   - Workaround: correct ownership, apply SELinux labels, or mount with appropriate flags.

6) OOMs and memory pressure during model load
   - Symptom: kernel OOM kills runtime or container; frequent restarts.
   - Quick checks: `dmesg | grep -i oom`, `kubectl describe pod` for OOM killed reasons, node memory utilization.
   - Workaround: increase instance memory, reduce batch sizes or quantize model, enable swap only as last resort.

Terraform module notes (practical reminders):
- Always run `terraform fmt` and `terraform validate` before sharing files with the customer.
- Keep module versions pinned in customer overlays. Don’t upgrade modules across an active release without a rollback plan.
- Use remote state with object versioning and lifecycle rules; keep at least 7 days of state snapshots.
- Use `-parallelism=1` for sensitive applies (stateful infra like block volume attachments) when in doubt.
- Prefer `terraform plan -out` and attach the plan to the incident. Capture diffs, especially resource replacements.
- Document provider upgrades in the module CHANGELOG and call out breaking changes.

Upgrade and rollback play notes (short):
- Preflight: run plan in a disposable workspace, run smoke tests in a staging cluster with identical TF variables and state snapshot.
- Canary: if possible, canary apply on a subset of nodes (use scale down plan or targeted module instances) and run full smoke tests.
- Rollback triggers: data loss risk, sustained service failure >5 minutes after full restart attempts, or CPU/GPU OOM >3 occurrences in 15 minutes.
- Rollback steps: restore tfstate snapshot to previous object version, re-run `terraform apply` with the prior release tag, restart runtime.
- Post‑rollback: rotate any credentials or temporary tokens used during the failed upgrade and document the exact repro steps.

Debugging artifacts to collect (minimum):
- terraform plan output, terraform apply logs, backend state snapshot (pulled copy), systemd/journalctl logs (last 5k lines), docker/k8s pod logs (previous + current), `nvidia-smi` output, `dmesg` tail, and `top`/`free -m`.

Escalation matrix (who to ping first):
- On‑call eng-private-deployments (primary SRE) — Slack #oncall-private + call on‑call phone.
- Infra-runtime lead (Ethan Brooks) for complex TF module or state issues.
- Runtime team (María López) for model serving crashes or GPU driver issues.
- Solutions eng for customer communication and temporary hosted fallback.

Notes & TODOs (local):
- Add exact systemd unit names for `redwood-runtime` variants per customer OS (Ubuntu 20.04 vs RHEL8).
- Add automated playbook for state snapshot and safe restore (one‑click script).
- Add specific vendor driver matrix for supported kernels and recommended driver versions.

Appendix: helpful snippets
- Safe pull of remote state: `terraform state pull > /tmp/remote-state-$(date +%s).tfstate`
- View locked state metadata: inspect backend object metadata in S3/GS/Azure to find locker details.
- Quick permission fix: `sudo chown -R redwood:redwood /var/lib/redwood` then `sudo restorecon -Rv /var/lib/redwood` (if SELinux).

If you used this doc during an incident, append a short incident note at the top with timestamp and which section you followed. Keep this file as ephemeral working notes — copy into the canonical Confluence runbook after stabilization.
